episode_title: The Brave New Future of Electricity

stories.title: David Foster Wallace's Fish Story
stories.description: Amit uses the 'This is Water' story (two young fish asking 'what is water?') to illustrate how we take electricity for granted—it's an unseen infrastructure we normalize.

stories.title: Ajay at the Coal Plant
stories.description: Ajay recounts visiting a coal power plant and asking them to 'spin up' quickly. The operators explained it takes hours, illustrating the inflexibility of old thermal power compared to the needs of a modern grid.

stories.title: The 1971 Oil Crisis Rumor
stories.description: Ajay investigates a rumor that Middle Eastern countries cut off oil to India during the 1971 war. He confirmed with a friend of the then-ambassador to Saudi Arabia that this was an urban legend; it never happened.

stories.title: Bhutan's Hydro Success
stories.description: A foreign policy success story where India builds and runs hydro plants in Bhutan, and Bhutan sells the power back to India. A win-win business arrangement.

stories.title: Nepal's Missed Opportunity
stories.description: In contrast to Bhutan, political mistrust between India and Nepal has prevented the development of Nepal's vast hydro potential, which could have powered North India's air conditioners in summer.

stories.title: Tamil Nadu's Offshore Wind Potential
stories.description: The 'North Sea' opportunity for India: vast offshore wind potential off the coast of Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka. It requires Tamil Nadu to fix its electricity policy and India/Sri Lanka to fix their foreign policy.

core_ideas.description: The old grid was centralized, government-run, and relied on steady coal/hydro. The new grid is decentralized, market-driven, and relies on variable solar/wind, requiring price signals to manage supply and demand.
Solar energy is abundant and cheap in the afternoon, but demand peaks in the evening when the sun is down. This mismatch is the central challenge of the modern grid.

The solution to the evening peak is not just engineering, but economics. Let prices fluctuate. Cheap afternoon electricity will encourage EV charging and storage; expensive evening electricity will encourage conservation and wind/storage supply.

Nuclear is the safest, cleanest, and most dense form of energy. Fears are based on old accidents (Chernobyl, Fukushima) which were due to specific failures (Soviet state, tsunami) not the technology itself. SMRs are the future.
Nationalism (Swadeshi) leads to inefficiency in energy. We should buy the best reactors (French/American) and trade energy with neighbors (Bhutan, Sri Lanka) based on business logic, not false pride.
Slang terms used to describe boring things ('blade') and slow understanding ('tubelight'), metaphorically applied to the Indian state's slow adaptation to the new energy reality.
